newsitem.title: UK: BT urges calm ahead of MCI review.
newsitem.headline: BT urges calm ahead of MCI review.

text.p: The chairman of British Telecom called for calm on Wednesday ahead of a thorough review of BT's U.S. merger partner MCI Communications Corp's strategy.

BT, whose planned $20 billion merger was rocked last week by an unexpected profit warning from MCI, denied newspaper reports that it was seeking two top-level resignations at America's second biggest long-distance carrier after last Thursday's surprise trading statement.

Instead, Sir Iain Vallance, BT's chairman, emphasised that BT would be working with MCI to decide how best to respond to what he called significant change in the U.S. telecoms market. In a show of confidence, he also praised the American company's "courage and skill" in breaking into new markets.

"The important thing at the moment is to take time to look sensibly and thoroughly at the U.S. market...be calm, analyse and act in shareholders' best interests," he told around 930 concerned shareholders at BT's annual meeting in the Scottish capital of Edinburgh.

BT also denied a Wall Street Journal report which said that under the merger terms any change in MCI's local U.S. business would not qualify as a "material adverse" event which could prompt renegotiation.

BT will be partly looking at whether MCI's investment plans in local U.S. markets, which will ring up higher than expected losses, can or should be altered and if the merger terms need to be re-negotiated to take account of a sharp fall in both BT and MCI's share price.
Both sides can of course still agree to walk away from the deal, an option which analysts say is unlikely.
"Until we have completed our review, we cannot give you explicit guidance as to the implications," Vallance told shareholders.
Asked how long the review was likely to take, a BT spokesman said: "How long is a piece of string?" He added that until the review was completed, BT could not comment on the future of the merger.
Bonfield and BT's finance director Robert Brace are heading for Washington this week.

Vallance, fielding a barrage of questions at the meeting from mainly small investors, attempted to assure his audience that the U.S. market and BT's relationship with MCI remained of key strategic importance.

But after conceding surprise and disappointment following MCI's forecasts last week of higher losses because of problems breaking into the $100 billion local U.S. telecoms market, he dismissed a suggestion that he was "an English muffin which Americans eat for breakfast".
"I look on myself more as a Scottish thistle than an English muffin," he said.
BT is paying a hefty premium for the 80 percent of MCI it does not already own.
MCI says its local U.S. market losses this year due to heavy investment could reach $800 million, twice previous forecasts, and 1998 losses could be even higher.
MCI blames delays by local U.S. telecom monopolies in opening up their markets and, along with BT, is calling on regulators for effective action against those who "thwart competition".
Some analysts say MCI's profit warning might be partly a political move to designed to put pressure on regulators to open up markets more quickly.
But an MCI spokeswoman in Edinburgh for the BT meeting denied these claims.
"It would have been a whole lot easier to have gone out and placed an advertisement - and less painful," the spokeswoman said.
Other analysts believe the MCI profit warnings may point to problems with its long-distance business.

Vallance, who was joined at the BT meeting by MCI chairman Bert Roberts, also dismissed a suggestion from one shareholder that chief executive Sir Peter Bonfield should step down because BT "appears not to have done its homework" before announcing what will be, regulators willing, the biggest transatlantic merger on record.

"There is no question of asking Sir Peter for his resignation," Vallance said, emphasising the fluid nature of U.S. telecom markets. He said information given to shareholders in April at an extraordinary meeting to approve the merger was the best available at the time.
"We never said it was going to be easy," added Bonfield.
BT's its review will be headed by Bonfield and the chief executive of MCI, Jerry Taylor. Brace is expected to be responsible for the number crunching.

Some analysts say BT and MCI were unwise not to heed a similar trading statement from MCI's its arch-rival, AT&T. AT&T, America's biggest telecoms company, warned in March that it was also having problems breaking into local markets.
Markets interpreted AT&T's warning more as a sign of managerial problems rather than drawing possible conclusions for MCI. "MCI had a different view of things at that time," conceded a BT spokesman.
BT and MCI plan to merge into a company called Concert Plc, a global telecommunications giant that wants to offer sophisticated services to high-margin corporate customers around the world.

Concert, which BT had promised would yield "tremendous growth opportunities", is still awaiting final regulatory clearance in the U.S. from the Federal Communications Commission. Definitive approval is expected around autumn.
